t: LeetCode 3127 — Make a Square with the Same Color
o: We have a fixed 3x3 grid of 'B'/'W' cells. We may recolor **at most one** cell, and want to know whether some 2x2 sub-square can then be monochromatic. There are only four possible 2x2 squares (top-left corners at (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1)). For each square, count how many cells differ from its majority color: if 0 mismatches it's already uniform; if exactly 1 mismatch we can fix it with our single change; if 2 or more, one change can't fix it. In Example 1 the top-left square has three 'B' and one 'W', so flipping that 'W' works → true. In Example 2 every 2x2 square is a 2-2 split (checkerboard), needing two changes → false. Example 3 already contains a uniform square → true. Since the grid size is constant, brute-force enumeration over the four squares is trivially fast.
k: There are only four 2x2 squares in a 3x3 grid; check each independently.
A square is achievable iff at most one of its four cells differs from the other cells' color (i.e., mismatch count vs majority ≤ 1).
Equivalently: a square works if some color appears ≥ 3 times among its 4 cells.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute force over all 2x2 squares
a.i: Enumerate each of the four 2x2 squares by its top-left corner (i, j) where i, j ∈ {0, 1}. Count occurrences of 'B' and 'W' inside it. If either count is ≥ 3, then either the square is already uniform (count 4) or a single flip makes it uniform (count 3), so return true. If no square qualifies, return false.
s: For each top-left corner (i, j) with i in {0,1} and j in {0,1}:
Count the number of 'B' cells among grid[i][j], grid[i][j+1], grid[i+1][j], grid[i+1][j+1].
If that count is 0 or ≥ 3 (equivalently max(countB, 4-countB) ≥ 3), return true.
After checking all four squares, return false.
a.t: O(1) — a fixed 3x3 grid means at most 4 squares × 4 cells = 16 checks.

a.n: Approach 2: Try every single cell change directly
a.i: Instead of counting per square, simulate: for each cell, tentatively flip its color and check whether any of the four 2x2 squares becomes uniform. This mirrors the problem statement literally ('change at most one cell') and also covers the case of changing zero cells automatically, since an already-uniform square stays uniform after any flip of an outside cell — but careful: flipping a cell inside a uniform square breaks it, so we must also allow 'no change'. Simplest correct variant: first check whether a uniform square already exists; otherwise try all 9 flips.
s: Write a helper that returns true if any 2x2 square is currently uniform.
Run the helper on the original grid; if true, return true (zero changes).
For each cell (i, j), flip grid[i][j] to the opposite color, run the helper, flip back.
Return true if any flip produced a uniform square, else false.
a.t: O(1) — 9 flips × 4 squares × 4 cells ≈ 144 checks, constant bounded.
a.sp: O(1) — flips are done in place and reverted.

w: Prefer Approach 1 in an interview: it is shorter, avoids mutation, and the key observation (a square is fixable iff one color appears ≥ 3 times, i.e., the split is not 2-2) is clean. Common pitfalls: forgetting that 'at most one' includes zero changes (Approach 1 handles this naturally since count 4 passes); miscounting which cells belong to a square when iterating top-left corners (bounds are i, j ∈ {0,1}, not {0..2}); and in Approach 2, forgetting to revert the flipped cell before continuing. Edge cases: fully uniform grids (trivially true) and perfect checkerboards (false). Follow-ups might generalize to n×m grids with k changes allowed — then you'd slide over all 2x2 windows and track minimum mismatches per window, answering whether min mismatch ≤ k.
